title: Itihasa: Epic as Story and Teaching
bigQuestion: How do the Ramayana and Mahabharata tell stories and teach dharma at the same time?

story.title: A Story Inside a Story
story.kicker: A storyteller opens one story, and inside it another, and inside that another.
paragraphs: In a forest called Naimisha, many sages have gathered for a long ritual. A traveling bard named Ugrashravas arrives. The sages welcome him and ask for a story. "Tell us the great tale," they say, "the one you heard at King Janamejaya's snake sacrifice."

So the bard begins. He tells how, years before, a sage named Vaishampayana told the tale to King Janamejaya. And Vaishampayana had learned it from his own teacher, Vyasa, who composed it. Vyasa was also a grandfather of the heroes in the story.

Inside the tale of the heroes, characters stop to tell stories of their own. A sage tells a sad prince about a king named Nala who lost everything at dice. A wife tells of Savitri, who followed Death. A grandfather lying on a bed of arrows teaches for days.

This is how the Mahabharata opens, according to its first book. Stories sit inside stories, like boxes inside boxes. Readers sometimes lose track of who is speaking. Yet each layer reminds them that the story was handed from voice to voice.

The Mahabharata even says of itself that what is found here may be found elsewhere, but what is not here is nowhere. Many readers take this as a proud claim that the epic holds all of life, from love and war to grief and wisdom.
story.think: Why might a storyteller put stories inside other stories? What does it do for the listener?

lessons.title: So It Was
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus call the Ramayana and Mahabharata itihasa, meaning 'so indeed it was', a genre of sacred history and epic.
reading: When a Hindu grandparent begins the Ramayana, they often speak as if telling true history. The Sanskrit word for the two great epics is *itihasa*. It comes from iti ha asa, which means 'so indeed it was.'

Many Hindus read the epics as history: real events in a distant age. Others read them mainly as sacred stories that teach dharma. Scholars study them as *epics*, long poems about heroes, gods, war and duty, which grew over centuries.

Itihasa belongs to smriti, the remembered texts. Yet the epics are hugely important. The Mahabharata calls itself a fifth Veda. For many Hindus, the epics are the most loved of all their texts, told at bedtime, on stage and on TV.

words.d: 'so indeed it was'; the Hindu name for the epics, the Ramayana and Mahabharata
a long poem or story about heroes, gods and great events
a kind or type of writing, such as epic, hymn or poem

lessons.title: Dates and Authors
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition names Valmiki and Vyasa as authors, while scholars date the epics' growth to about 400 BCE–400 CE.
reading: Hindu tradition says the sage *Valmiki* composed the Ramayana and is honored as the first poet. It says the sage *Vyasa* composed the Mahabharata and also arranged the Vedas. In the traditional view, the events took place in very ancient ages.
Scholars see the epics as growing over many centuries. Most date their main growth to roughly 400 BCE to 400 CE. They point to layers in the text: some parts seem older, some added later.

Both views are held with care. A Hindu reader may honor Valmiki as the poet while also enjoying the work of scholars. This course names both views and does not decide between them. Remember to use 'c.' for these dates.

words.d: the sage whom Hindu tradition names as composer of the Ramayana, honored as the first poet
the sage whom Hindu tradition names as composer of the Mahabharata

lessons.title: Frame Stories
lessons.mainIdea: Both epics use frame stories, where one story is told inside another.
reading: A *frame story* is a story that holds other stories, like a picture frame. The Mahabharata has at least three frames. A bard tells sages in the Naimisha forest. Inside, Vaishampayana tells King Janamejaya. Inside that, the heroes' story unfolds.

The Ramayana has a frame too. In its first book, Valmiki hears Rama's story from the sage Narada. Later he sees a hunter kill a bird, and his grief flows out in a new kind of verse, the shloka. The god Brahma then asks him to tell Rama's story in that verse.
Frames do several jobs. They show who passed the story down. They let characters pause to teach. They also remind readers that the tale is being told, and that listening is part of it.

words.d: a story that holds other stories told inside it
a Sanskrit verse form; tradition says Valmiki first spoke it in grief
a traveling storyteller or poet

lessons.title: The Eighteen Parvas
lessons.mainIdea: The Mahabharata is arranged in eighteen books, called parvas, that trace a family feud from its start to its end.
reading: The Mahabharata tells of two sets of cousins, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. They quarrel over a kingdom. The epic follows them from birth, through a dice game and exile, to a great war and its sad aftermath.

The story is arranged in eighteen *parvas*, or books. The first is the Adi Parva, the book of beginnings. The Sabha Parva holds the dice game. The Bhishma Parva holds the Bhagavad Gita. The last books tell of the heroes' final journey.

Eighteen shows up again and again. The war lasts eighteen days, eighteen armies fight, and the Gita has eighteen chapters. Many readers notice this pattern. Scholars also note a list of a hundred smaller sections, the upaparvas.

words.d: one of the eighteen books of the Mahabharata
the five brothers who are the heroes of the Mahabharata

lessons.title: The Seven Kandas
lessons.mainIdea: Valmiki's Ramayana has seven kandas, or books, that follow Rama from birth to his reign.
reading: Valmiki's Ramayana has seven *kandas*. The Bala Kanda tells of Rama's childhood. Ayodhya Kanda tells of his exile. Aranya Kanda, the forest book, includes Sita's capture. Kishkindha Kanda tells of the monkey kingdom.

Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book, follows Hanuman to Lanka. Yuddha Kanda tells of the war. Uttara Kanda, the last book, tells of Rama's reign and of Sita's later trials. Many scholars think the first and last books were added later than the middle five.
Many Hindus read the Sundara Kanda on its own as a devotional text. Some families recite it in times of trouble. This shows that a part of an epic can take on its own life in worship.

words.d: one of the seven books of the Ramayana
the 'beautiful book' of the Ramayana, about Hanuman's journey to Lanka

lessons.title: Stories Inside the Mahabharata
lessons.mainIdea: The Mahabharata holds many side stories, like Nala and Damayanti and Savitri, that teach about love and duty.
reading: During the Pandavas' forest exile, sages tell them stories to comfort and teach them. In one, King *Nala* loses his kingdom at dice and wanders the forest. His wife *Damayanti* never gives up, and at last they are reunited.

The Pandavas, too, have lost everything at dice. So the story mirrors their own, and it gives them hope that loss is not the end. Readers see how the epic uses side stories to hold up a mirror to the main characters.

Another tale tells of *Savitri*, who follows Yama, the lord of death, as he carries away her husband's life. With wisdom and persistence, she wins it back. Many Hindu women honor Savitri in a yearly fast called Vat Savitri.

words.d: a king in a Mahabharata side story who loses his kingdom at dice
Nala's faithful wife, who searches for him
a wife in the Mahabharata who wins her husband's life back from Yama

lessons.title: Hard Choices About Dharma
lessons.mainIdea: The epics show characters facing hard choices about dharma, and they often leave readers to think it through.
reading: In the Sabha Parva, Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, gambles away his kingdom, his brothers, himself and finally his wife, *Draupadi*. She is dragged into the hall. She asks the elders: did he lose himself first? If so, could he still wager me?

The elders fall silent. Even the wise Bhishma says dharma here is subtle. The epic does not give an easy answer. It lets the question hang in the air. The Mahabharata often says that dharma is subtle and hard to know.

The Ramayana tends to show clearer models, like Rama keeping his father's promise. Yet it has hard moments too. Both epics invite readers to argue about what the right action was. Many Hindu families and scholars do exactly that.

words.d: wife of the five Pandavas, who questions the elders after the dice game

lessons.title: Kings, Friends and Loss
lessons.mainIdea: Besides dharma, the epics teach about kingship, friendship and grief.
reading: The epics are full of friendships: Rama and Hanuman, Krishna and Arjuna, Rama and the monkey king Sugriva. They also show friendships that lead to harm, like Duryodhana and Karna, bound by loyalty even to a wrong cause.

The epics teach about kingship. The Shanti Parva, the book of peace, has Bhishma, dying on a bed of arrows, teach Yudhishthira how to rule. In the Ramayana, Rama's reign, *Ramrajya*, became an ideal of just rule. Gandhi used the word for a fair society.
The epics do not hide grief. After the war, the Mahabharata's women weep over the dead in the Stri Parva. Readers often say the epic's ending feels like mourning, not victory, even for the winners.

words.d: the rule of Rama; an ideal of just and peaceful government
the 'book of peace' in the Mahabharata, where Bhishma teaches about ruling

look.title: A Loyal Friend

look.prompt: Is Karna's loyalty a strength, a flaw, or both? What might the epic be teaching?

lessons.title: Ganguli and Griffith in English
lessons.mainIdea: K.M. Ganguli's full English Mahabharata (1883–96) and Griffith's Ramayan (1870–74) are public-domain translations.
reading: The Mahabharata is enormous. The first complete English prose translation was published in Calcutta between 1883 and 1896. It is credited to *Kisari Mohan Ganguli*, and it was first issued by the publisher Pratap Chandra Roy.
Ralph T.H. Griffith, who later translated the Rig Veda, translated Valmiki's Ramayana into English verse, published 1870–74 as The Ramayan of Valmiki. Both works are now in the public domain.

Scholars later made Critical Editions of both epics by comparing many manuscripts. The Pune edition of the Mahabharata took from 1919 to 1966. Newer translations are based on these. Older ones remain useful because they are free to read and quote.

words.d: translator credited with the first full English Mahabharata (1883–96)
a scholarly text made by comparing many manuscripts

lessons.title: Many Ramayanas
lessons.mainIdea: The Ramayana has been retold in many languages, including Kamban's Tamil version and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.
reading: Valmiki's Sanskrit Ramayana is not the only one. In the 12th century (c.), the poet *Kamban* retold it in Tamil as the Ramavataram. Kamban's Rama is more clearly divine, and his poetry is loved across Tamil Nadu.

In the 16th century, *Tulsidas* retold it in Awadhi, a form of Hindi, as the *Ramcharitmanas*, the lake of Rama's deeds. It is full of bhakti, loving devotion to Rama. In North India, it is the Ramayana many families know best and recite at home.

There are versions in Bengali, Telugu, Malayalam and many other languages, and in Thailand, Indonesia and beyond. Jain and Buddhist tellings exist too. Scholars speak of many Ramayanas, each with its own emphasis.
